properties.Site name: Risingham 1, Corsenside - north side of R.Rede c.1820
properties.Inscription Translation: N/A
properties.Notes:
The Northumberland HER quotes Hodgson (1827) as follows: �A few years ago (c.1820) the Rede tore away part of a meadow on its north side, exposing two round pillars standing upright, about 12 feet apart, apparently on each side of the road where the (north?) end of the old bridge might have been. One of the pillars is now used as a gatepost to the garden of the inn at West Woodburn and the other at the Wood House, a quarter of a mile north of that village.�  Note that Hodgson does not say that the stones were from the bridge as is usually stated today, merely that they might have been near its north end, however he did not allow for movement of the river since the Roman period, the river at that time being probably over 200m to the south. Please note that Mackenzie�s account, from his second edition of c.1853, only mentions one of these two stones, the other one he refers to is the High House stone, now lost.
The two stones are referred to as here as Risingham 1 & 2 � both are extant. 
Risingham 1. In 1956, this stone was supporting the roof of a shed immediately west of the farmhouse at High Leam. It was relocated in 1971 by the Redesdale Society, and is now at NY 88878772 next to a round cairn and included in its scheduling ( monument number 21037). It is roughly cylindrical, with a squared base below ground level, standing 1.8m above ground, its width varying in diameter from 0.45m to 0.5m. 
Risingham 2. The Northumberland HER states that one stone now stands in the garden immediately southeast of the Bay Horse Inn, having formerly served as a gatepost, however that location has not been confirmed. In 1956, the O.S. field investigator described the stone as having a diameter of 0.3m with 1.55m of its height above ground level. When the pillar was removed to its present position the base was found to be roughly square and not dressed. There is a cylindrical recess 0.5m below the top of the pillar which is grooved by the weather.

A Roman milestone was found in 1919 at Trethevey. It measures 1.4m in height and is 0.3m square and has been damaged as a result of being used as a gatepost. Though its original site seems to be unknown it now stands in the garden of St Pirans, opposite the chapel. The date of the inscription is 251 - 253 when Volusian was Emperor. The stone is Scheduled and is very eroded. It has now been moved to a nursery garden . The monument was included in the Schedule on 26/11/1928, the scheduling affirmed on 8/12/1997 and revised on 24/7/1998.
The monument was subject to a conservation project in 2008-9 which involved removing the iron gate fittings and damaging ironwork, and setting the stone in a granite base in a new position in the verge outside of the garden boundary of St Piran's. A plaque was fixed to the garden wall nearby.

It has been variously regarded as a boundary marker, a broken cross shaft, and a Roman milestone - the latter is currently more favoured based apparently on its morphology and 'proximity' to a Roman road. If this is true, however, it must have been moved at least a kilometer from RR4e, unless of course there is a currently unknown branch road from RR4e running past the stone, which is possible. Also, it appears not to be known whether the base is cylindrical, or squared, as would be expected with a Roman stone. Sedgeley did not include it in his gazetteer

It was found in the ruins of a villa, now beneath modern Worthing and it seems probable that it was brought to the villa from elsewhere, possibly from RR153 which is thought (without much evidence) to run across the northern edge of Worthing.

There is no clear evidence for a Roman road heading due west from Silchester, and it seems most likely it was removed from either RR4b or RR41a and reused as a boundary marker - the Hampshire / Berkshire boundary runs along Silchester Road.

properties.Notes: This milestone was found in Beancroft road in about 1880. The stone was originally dedicated to Trajan Decius and his son Herennius Decius (although neither of those names are used in the inscription), probably in AD250. When both Decius and his son were killed at the battle of Abritus in AD251, it seems the good people of Castleford were keen to keep in with the new regime, turning the stone upside down and adding a second inscription dedicated to the new co-emperors, Gallus and Volusian. The second inscription also gives the distance to York, which is given as 22 miles, one mile more than the distance given in the Antonine itineraries, which may be measuring to a point on the northern edge of the settlement.

Half Acres covers quite a large area, including the findspot of Castleford's other milestone, and it is therefore quite reasonable to suggest that the findspots were very close together, the two stones both marking the twenty second mile from York.

properties.Form: Rough Cylinder, slightly oval in section
properties.Notes: The name 'Duel Cross', a corruption of 'Devil's Cross' is thought to derive from the stone, and shows the stone to have been found pretty much in situ. A second Yorkshire stone has a similar name, the Diallstone from RR712 and now in Slaithwaite. Found in 1776, the stone had two inscriptions, the first being almost entirely erased before a dedication to Decius was added. The last four letters XXC |S are problematic and omitted from the RIB Edition. XX could be a distance to a place beginning with �C�, except Duel Cross isn�t 20 miles from anywhere significant. There is a solution, but only if the mason did not fully understand the rules of Roman numerals; could XXC have meant 80 miles (shorter to carve than LXXX)? This would work well, since Corbridge is actually 81 miles away. The S is at a different line spacing, is 19mm higher than the other letters, and is centrally placed, so may not be part of the Secondary inscription at all, possibly part of the original primary inscription or added later.

properties.Notes: The stone stands next to RR72b, and is traditionally regarded as a Roman milestone. The degree of weathering is severe, suggesting extreme age, and the possibility of a prehistoric origin cannot be ruled out, especially as the setting out of RR72b suggests it is based on a pre-existing route. It is of a similar scale to the stone on the Stanegate north of Vindolanda.

properties.Site name: The Dial Stone, Booth Bank Clough
properties.Inscription Translation: N/A
properties.Notes: This stone was found in Booth Bank Clough in the mid 16th century, then transported for about a mile to the grounds of Slaithwaite Manor House. Apart from a brief excursion to the Isle of Man, the stone has lived there ever since. It is far too broad to be a medieval cross as has often been claimed, and the fact that RR712 is now known to have crossed Booth Bank Clough leaves no doubt that this is indeed a Roman milestone

properties.Notes: This stone has only be assessed from a single photograph, so conclusions have to be tentative. It is certainly similar to the Dial Stone in Slaithwaite, and may even be slightly larger, and would have only had to make a 2km journey, entirely downhill, from RR712. However, it is slightly concerning that the vertical edge is very straight - perhaps too straight. Also the photo shows several parallel striations at about 45 degrees to the orientation of the stone - these could be bedding planes, but could also suggest that the stone has been cut relatively recently.

The stone is very badly eroded, and had apparently been re-used as a threshold in a late Roman building. It was found during the excavation of a Roman site near North Lodge Farm in the late 1970's or early 1980's.Sometimes described as a 'failed attempt to make a milestone' there is no reason to say this - all damage is later.

properties.Inscription Translation: unknown
properties.Notes: The former existence of this milestone comes for the bounds of an Anglo Saxon charter, S.142, which is the only known charter mentioning a 'Mila Stane', which the bounds surveyor used as convenient marker. The location was deduced by G.B. Grundy, however he was assuming that the modern parish boundary was at this point the same as the 8th century boundary, which may not be the case. If Grundy was correct, it suggests that RR194(x) turned east to head to Droitwich. If, however, it was 800m to the WSW (at about SO78446310), which also fits the boundary description, then the road was clearly headed to Worcester.
